title: Charity is patient (1 Corinthians 13:1–7)
hook: charity is patient, is kind, envieth not

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eye and the hand, and one body with no spare parts. Your line was the hand needs the eye. Who did you thank, and for what gift? Day five hundred seventy-four.

It's often read at weddings, so it's easy to assume it was written for one. It wasn't. Paul was writing to a church that was quarreling: over which leader to follow, over food, over who had the most impressive spiritual gift. Right in the middle of his argument about gifts, he stops. I'll show you, he says, a more excellent way. And then he writes the passage that has long outlived the quarrel.
screen: `WRITTEN FOR A WEDDING?` → `NO: FOR A CHURCH IN A FIGHT.` → `A MORE EXCELLENT WAY.`

segments.voice: He begins by making every gift worthless without it: "If I speak with the tongues of men, and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." Then he describes charity, and notice he doesn't describe a feeling. He lists what it does and what it won't do: "Charity is patient, is kind: charity envieth not, dealeth not perversely; is not puffed up." It isn't ambitious, doesn't seek its own, isn't provoked to anger, thinks no evil. Then four alls: "Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things." Why does the Douay-Rheims say charity and not love? Paul's Greek word is agapē. Saint Jerome's Latin Bible rendered it caritas, and the Douay-Rheims followed the Latin. So, here, did the King James. Newer English translations tend to say love. In everyday English, charity has shrunk to mean giving money. In Catholic teaching it keeps the old, large meaning. The Catechism calls charity the virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbor as ourselves for the love of God. Some readers try a simple exercise: read the passage again with their own name where it says charity. Patient, kind, not puffed up. The first line is the hard one. And that first line matters. Of everything Paul could have put first, he put patience.
screen: `WITHOUT IT: SOUNDING BRASS.` · `NOT A FEELING: WHAT IT DOES.` · `AGAPĒ, CARITAS, CHARITY.` · `PUT YOUR OWN NAME IN.` · then, large: `CHARITY IS PATIENT, IS KIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse patience. Settle, and breathe. Think of the place you're most likely to lose patience today. A slow line. A child who won't put on shoes. A coworker who explains the same thing twice. Picture it happening, and notice whatever starts to rise. Now picture yourself waiting it out, one breath longer than usual, and saying nothing sharp. Just once. If you pray, you can say the line charity is patient, is kind, slowly, as a prayer. If you don't, just rest in that one longer breath. The bell holds the time.
Charity. The Douay-Rheims word for Paul's agapē: love that gives itself. The first thing he says it is: patient. Today's word.

Your line: one breath longer. Today, wait one breath longer than usual before responding, and notice it. And that's week eighty-two: reasonable service, moria, coadjutors, a temple, commemoration, one body, and charity. Day five hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Catholics count charity as one of the three theological virtues with faith and hope, and 1 Corinthians 13 is one of the readings couples may choose for a Catholic wedding.

fork.setup: you're Paul, mid-argument with a church fighting over whose gift is greatest. what comes next in your letter?
options: rank the gifts from best to worst.
tell them gifts don't matter at all.
show them a more excellent way: charity.
fork.reveal: he stops the argument and writes about charity: without it, even the tongues of angels are sounding brass.

original.note: Greek: love. rendered caritas in Jerome's Latin, and charity in the Douay-Rheims.

trapdoor: what you thought: charity means giving money.
what it means: in Paul and in Catholic teaching, charity is love itself, the patient, kind love of God and neighbor.
what a scholar hears: agapē, rendered caritas by Jerome; the English word kept the Latin, then shrank in everyday use to almsgiving.
